name: Consistent Hashing
intent: Assign keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys, instead of reshuffling almost everything.
scenario: A cache cluster has three servers and spreads keys across them. When a fourth server is added, almost every key would change servers with the obvious approach, emptying the cache.
problem: The simple way to pick a server is hash(key) mod N. It balances well, but N appears in the formula, so changing N changes the answer for most keys. Going from 3 to 4 servers moves about 75 percent of the keys. For a cache that means most lookups suddenly miss; for a sharded database it means moving most of the data.

howItWorks.title: Place servers on a ring
howItWorks.text: Hash each server's name to a position on a circle that wraps around from the highest hash value back to zero. The servers now sit at fixed points on the ring.

howItWorks.title: Place keys on the same ring
howItWorks.text: Hash each key onto the ring too. The key belongs to the first server found by walking clockwise from the key's position.

howItWorks.title: Adding a server takes keys from one neighbour
howItWorks.text: A new server lands at one point on the ring and takes over only the keys between it and the previous server. Every other key keeps its owner. On average that is about 1/N of the keys.

howItWorks.title: Removing a server hands its keys to the next one
howItWorks.text: When a server leaves or fails, its keys go to the next server clockwise. Nothing else moves.

howItWorks.title: Virtual nodes smooth out the balance
howItWorks.text: With few points the arcs are uneven, so one server can own far more than its share. Giving each server many virtual nodes (for example 100 positions on the ring) evens out the load, and spreads a removed server's keys across many others.

pros: Resizing a cluster moves only about 1/N of the keys
No central lookup table is needed: every client computes the owner
A failed node's load spreads across the survivors
Used for caches, sharded stores and load balancing with affinity
cons: More complex than modulo hashing, and a bit slower to look up
Needs virtual nodes to balance well, which costs memory
Hot keys still land on a single node
Moved keys still have to be copied or re-fetched
whenToUse: Distributed caches where nodes come and go
Sharded databases and key-value stores that need to grow without mass migration
Load balancing where the same key should keep reaching the same server
whenNotToUse: A fixed set of servers that will not change: modulo is simpler
Tiny clusters where moving some keys does not matter
When you need range queries over keys: hashing destroys key order
pitfalls: Using too few virtual nodes and ending up with badly unbalanced servers
Using a weak hash function that clusters similar keys together
Forgetting that the language's default string hash may change between runs
Not planning how moved keys get transferred when the ring changes

quiz.question: A cache fleet of 4 nodes picks a node with hash(key) mod 4 and spreads keys evenly. You add a fifth node. Roughly what share of keys changes owner under modulo, and under a consistent-hash ring?
options: About 80 percent under modulo, about 20 percent on a ring.
About 20 percent under both schemes, since only the new node receives any keys at all.
About 80 percent under both, since every key is rehashed on a resize.
About 25 percent under modulo, and none on a ring.
quiz.explanation: With modulo, N is in the formula, so most keys land on a different node when N goes from 4 to 5. On a ring the new node only takes the arc between itself and its neighbour, about 1/5 of the keys. A ring still moves some keys, so none is wrong.

quiz.question: A ring has 3 servers, each hashed to a single position. Server A owns about 55 percent of keys, and when server C later fails, all of its keys land on one neighbour. Which change fixes both problems?
options: Switch to a stronger hash function for the server names, so positions are spread more randomly.
Add a fourth server that also has a single position.
Move the heaviest server's position by hand when skew shows up.
Give each server around 100 virtual nodes spread across the ring.
quiz.explanation: With few points on the ring, arcs are uneven whatever the hash. Many virtual nodes per server even out the share and spread a failed server's keys across many survivors. A better hash or one more point still leaves very few arcs.

quiz.question: A team builds a ring correctly and places keys using their language's built-in string hash in each client process. After a rolling restart of the clients, cache hit rate drops close to zero though no cache node changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: Restarted clients rebuild the ring with fewer virtual nodes than before, so most keys land on other nodes.
Walking clockwise breaks when a client restarts, so keys go to the wrong neighbour and lookups miss on the node that owns them.
The default string hash differs between processes, so clients map keys to new ring positions.
The deploy resized the ring, which moved most keys and evicted the cached entries.
quiz.explanation: Many languages salt their default string hash per process, so two clients can disagree on where a key lives, and new clients disagree with the cached data. Use a stable hash such as murmur or xxhash. The ring itself and the nodes did not change.
